_comment: Upstream end-of-security-support dates, per branch. The index carries them so the GUI can warn
on a version nobody patches any more. It does not carry them so anything can be hidden: PHP is
offered from 7.0 upwards on purpose, which is years past every date below, because the people
who reach for a local development environment rather than a container are very often the people
maintaining something old. A warning is the honest answer; refusing to install is not.
_node_comment: Node.js lines are keyed by major, not by major.minor: a Node release line is 22, and 22.11 is
a patch of it. That is why mkindex.py looks a version up both ways. Dates are nodejs/Release's
own schedule.json. The odd-numbered lines are Current and last about eight months, which is why
several of them are already past — they are here so an index entry for one is marked rather
_python_comment: python.org's own release schedule: five years from a line's first release, ending in October.
Keyed by major.minor because that is what a Python release line is. 3.9 is here and is not
offered — python-build-standalone's current releases stop at 3.10 — so the entry exists only to
keep an older artifact of it dated rather than silently undated if one is ever republished.
_ruby_comment: ruby-lang.org's branch page: normal maintenance for about two years, security maintenance for
about a year and a half after that, and every line ends on 31 March. 3.1 is past even the
one-year grace this project allows and is not offered; it is dated here because RubyInstaller
still publishes it and an artifact that exists should not be undated.
_caddy_comment: Caddy has no entry, and the absence is deliberate rather than pending. The project publishes
no end-of-life schedule: there is one supported line, 2.x, and support means the newest patch
of it. A date invented here would be worse than none — the GUI would warn about a version that
is perfectly current, or stay silent about one that is not, and either way it would be this
file's opinion rather than upstream's. `mkindex.py` leaves a package undated when its kind is
absent, which is the honest answer.
The same will be true of every service whose publisher rolls support forward instead of
branching it; the ones that do branch — MariaDB and PostgreSQL both publish dated release
series — get entries when they are packed.
